You need to *read* all three; you'll *write* mostly the first one: | Tool | Job | Returns | |---|---|---| | `$` | one column, **by name** | a vector | | `[rows, cols]` | a rectangle, by position/name | usually a data frame | | `[[ ]]` | one element, dug out | the thing itself | **LM4 — `$`, the workhorse (5 min).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM4: a column is a vector airquality$Temp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 67 72 74 62 56 66 65 59 61 69 74 69 66 68 58 64 66 57 68 62 59 73 61 61 57 [26] 58 57 67 81 79 76 78 74 67 84 85 79 82 87 90 87 93 92 82 80 79 77 72 65 73 [51] 76 77 76 76 76 75 78 73 80 77 83 84 85 81 84 83 83 88 92 92 89 82 73 81 91 [76] 80 81 82 84 87 85 74 81 82 86 85 82 86 88 86 83 81 81 81 82 86 85 87 89 90 [101] 90 92 86 86 82 80 79 77 79 76 78 78 77 72 75 79 81 86 88 97 94 96 94 91 92 [126] 93 93 87 84 80 78 75 73 81 76 77 71 71 78 67 76 68 82 64 71 81 69 63 70 77 [151] 75 76 68 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(airquality$Temp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 77.88235 ``` ::: ::: > *YT2 (5 min). ➕ Insert a chunk. Using `$`, find:* > *(a) the mean of Wind;* > *(b) the max Temp;* > *(c) the mean of Ozone — it comes back `NA`. Fix it with the argument you > looked up in the help page last week;* > *(d) how many days had Temp above 90? (Hint: `sum(airquality$Temp > 90)` — > TRUE counts as 1.)* > *(a) ____ · (b) ____ · (c) ____ · (d) ____* **LM5 — `[rows, columns]` and `[[ ]]`, in one pass (5 min).** Predict each before running. Square brackets take a *position or a name*; double brackets dig out *one thing*: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM5: predict, then run airquality[1, ] # first row, all columns ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Switch to `iris`. Write ONE line for each:* > *(a) the Species column as a vector — how long is it?* > *(b) rows 51–53, all columns — what species are they?* > *(c) the last row of iris (use `nrow()` inside the brackets — no > hard-coded 150).* {{< vspace 1.5rem >}} # 3 · The pipe `|>` — the symbol you'll type more than any other (15 min) ::: {.callout-important title="Read this one out loud"} **`|>` means "and then."** Take the thing on the left, hand it to the function on the right. That's it. Everything from Monday on — every ETV cycle, every plot, every summary — is a chain of *and then*s. ::: **LM6 — the same code, two ways (5 min).** Question: *on average, how warm were the July days?* Without the pipe, you read this **inside-out**, from the deepest parentheses to the outermost: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM6a: nested — read from the INSIDE out round(mean(airquality$Temp[airquality$Month == 7]), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 83.9 ``` ::: ::: With the pipe, you read it **top-to-bottom, like a recipe**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM6b: piped — read "and then", top to bottom airquality$Temp[airquality$Month == 7] |> mean() |> round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 83.9 ``` ::: ::: Same answer. But the second one you can *say*: "take July's temperatures, **and then** average them, **and then** round to one decimal." ::: {.callout-note title="How the pipe works — the one rule"} - `x |> f()` is exactly `f(x)`. The left side becomes the **first argument** of the function on the right - `x |> f(y)` is `f(x, y)` — extra arguments go where they always did - So `airquality$Temp |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)` is `mean(airquality$Temp, na.rm = TRUE)` - Keyboard: **Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + M** types `|>` for you in Positron - Style: one step per line, indent the continuation. Your eye follows the recipe ::: **LM7 — a real chain (4 min).** Which days are missing Ozone? Read each line as "and then": ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM7: WHICH rows are missing Ozone? — read it as a sentence airquality$Ozone |> is.na() |> which() |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 10 25 26 27 32 ``` ::: ::: > *YT4 (6 min). ➕ Insert a chunk. Rewrite each nested line as a pipe, one > step per line, and confirm the answer doesn't change:* > *(a) `sqrt(mean(airquality$Wind))`* > *(b) `round(mean(airquality$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`* > *(c) `length(unique(iris$Species))`* > *Then write ONE pipe of your own: three steps, any data, and a comment > reading it as a sentence.* {{< vspace 1.5rem >}} # 4 · How big is data? (13 min) **LM8 — the ladder (4 min).** Data size is measured in **bytes** — one byte is roughly one letter. Every step up the ladder multiplies by a thousand: ![Each step is ×1,000. A byte is a letter; a kilobyte is a paragraph; a megabyte is a photo; a gigabyte is an hour of video; a terabyte is a whole laptop.](/assets/byte_ladder.svg){fig-alt="Ladder of storage units from byte to terabyte, each step ×1,000, with an everyday example on each step." width="100%"} **LM9 — where real things land (4 min).** The bars below are on a *log* scale — each gridline is another ×1,000. Notice where **your laptop's memory** sits, because that's the ceiling for what R can hold: ![Real-world sizes on a log scale, from one letter to a national census. The orange "laptop memory" bar is the amount of data R can hold at once.](/assets/how_big_is_it.svg){fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart on a log scale showing sizes of everyday things: a text message (bytes), a survey CSV (KB), a song (MB), an hour of HD video (GB), a laptop's RAM (8–16 GB), a laptop drive (512 GB), and a census extract (1 TB)." width="100%"} | Unit | ≈ bytes | Something you own that's about that size | |---|---|---| | **byte** | 1 | one letter of a text message | | **kilobyte (KB)** | 1 thousand | a long email; this class's survey as a `.csv`; `airquality` (5.6 KB) | | **megabyte (MB)** | 1 million | one phone photo (3 MB); one song (4 MB); a year of CA crime data (~100 MB) | | **gigabyte (GB)** | 1 billion | an hour of HD Netflix (3 GB); your laptop's **memory** (8–16 GB) | | **terabyte (TB)** | 1 trillion | two of your laptop's drives; a full US census extract | | **petabyte (PB)** | 1 quadrillion | Netflix's entire catalog; the data behind a weather forecast | Now measure **our** objects: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM9: how big are OUR objects? object.size(airquality) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5632 bytes ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} object.size(iris) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 7256 bytes ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} object.size(mtcars) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 7208 bytes ``` ::: ::: > *Q5. Order the three from smallest to largest, and name the unit they're > in: ____* **Why it matters (3 min):** R holds data **in memory** — the orange bar, not the red one. A 2 GB file on an 8 GB laptop imports (barely); a 200 GB file does not — you'd need different tools (a database, or a bigger machine). File size is the first thing to check *before* importing, which is exactly where next week begins. > *Q6. Your laptop has 8 GB of memory.
